summary: Describes a technique for sending radio pages through Internet mail infrastructure, focusing on pagers identified by international telephone numbers. It documents technical procedures for the TPC.INT subdomain. It is informational.

eli5.summary: You send an email to a special address with a phone number, and it makes someone's pager beep.

subtitle: How to send a radio page by email, using a pager's telephone number turned into a tpc.int domain name.

tldr.problem: Radio pagers are identified by telephone numbers, and there was no standard way to reach one using ordinary Internet mail.
tldr.mechanism: The telephone number is reversed digit by digit into a domain name under tpc.int, mail is routed to a paging server with MX records, and the local part of the address says what kind of pager it is.
tldr.outcome: An Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1569 and gives the technical procedures for the TPC.INT subdomain.

facts.label: Local part limit
facts.value: No more than 70 or so characters

today: RFC 1703 is an Informational memo from October 1994 that obsoletes RFC 1569. According to the metadata for this page it has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Radio paging is a one-way text notification service, useful alongside the usual two-way electronic mail. This memo describes how to do it through the Internet mail infrastructure, focusing on pagers that are identified through the international telephone network.

The technique maps telephone numbers to domain names and comes from the TPC.INT subdomain. For the overview and policy, the memo points to RFC 1530.
sections.eli5: A pager is a small gadget that beeps and shows a message. This memo shows how to send it a message by email.

sections.title: Naming and Addressing
sections.content:
A pager is identified by a telephone number such as +1 415 940 8776, where +1 is the country code. A PIN may also be needed to identify the pager uniquely.

The recipient address is made of a local part and a domain part. The domain part is built by reversing the telephone number, turning each digit into a domain label, and placing it under tpc.int. The number must not include international access codes. The local part is one of pager.ATOM, pager-alpha.ATOM or pager-numeric, where ATOM is an RFC 822 atom, an opaque string used to identify the recipient to the paging network.

The mailbox syntax is deliberately restricted, and because some mail software limits mailbox strings, the local part should be kept to no more than 70 or so characters.
sections.eli5: The phone number is written backwards with dots between the digits, and 'tpc.int' goes on the end. That backwards number is the address of the helper computer.

sections.title: Routing with MX Records
sections.content:
Messages are routed like any other mail, using the MX algorithm from RFC 974. A paging server may reach many pagers, so DNS wildcards are used. A server at dbc.mtview.ca.us that will handle any pager with the prefix +1 415 940 would have the record *.0.4.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int. IN MX 10 dbc.mtview.ca.us.

Several servers for one prefix get several MX records, and the TPC.INT DNS servers rotate the order for rudimentary load balancing. A matching wildcard does not mean the phone number is valid or that a pager exists. It only means that a server is willing to try.
sections.eli5: The internet looks up the backwards number like a signpost that points to the right helper computer. If several helpers can do the job, they take turns.

sections.title: Procedure for Alphanumeric and Numeric Pagers
sections.content:
The sender builds an RFC 822 message with a Message-ID field and text content, then mails it to the paging server. The server first reads the local part.

For pager.ATOM or pager-alpha.ATOM, the pager is alphanumeric, and ATOM names a carrier, a PIN, or both. If it is all digits, it is a PIN and the domain refers to the carrier's IXO access number. If it has no hyphen, it is a carrier name looked up in a local database. If it has a hyphen, the part before the first hyphen is the carrier and the part after is the PIN.

With pager. the page is the body of the message. With pager-alpha. the server decides which headers and body to use, for example it may look at To and Subject. For pager-numeric, the pager dials the telephone number from the domain part and the body must consist solely of digits.
sections.eli5: The first part of the address tells the helper what kind of pager it is. Letter pagers get words, and number pagers only get numbers.

sections.title: MAIL versus SEND, and Latency
sections.content:
A paging server MUST support the SMTP MAIL command and MAY support SEND, SOML or SAML. After MAIL, a positive reply means the message is at least queued for the paging network. After SEND, it means the paging network accepted it for delivery. After SOML or SAML, it means it may have been accepted.

Internet mail can add delays of minutes, hours or days through relays. A client that connects directly to the paging server, so that delivery is one SMTP hop, and uses only SEND or SAML, is assured that a positive reply means the page has been sent on the radio paging network.
sections.eli5: Normal email is like a letter that may sit in several post offices. If you hand your message straight to the pager company and ask for 'send now', you find out right away if it worked.

sections.title: Examples and Server Setup
sections.content:
The examples use the iddd.tpc.int subdomain, where a name like 14159408776.iddd.tpc.int is automatically treated as 6.7.7.8.0.4.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int. One MIME example mails pager-alpha.98765@18005551234.iddd.tpc.int, and a non-MIME one mails pager-numeric@14159408776.iddd.tpc.int with the body 2026282044.

The memo then walks through a hypothetical carrier, Pigeon Paging. It registers a domain, runs paging servers that implement SEND, has MX records added to TPC.INT with costs reflecting service quality, may offer a client using SEND, and may give customers mailboxes that map to the TPC.INT address. The only security note is that Internet mail may be monitored by third parties, in particular message relays.
sections.eli5: The memo shows sample messages and then imagines a pretend company, Pigeon Paging, setting up its computers. It also warns that other people along the way could peek at email.
